one_liner: Non-flambda ocamlopt (OCaml 5.4.1) running benchLANG binary trees 14% faster than per-node malloc/free C and 25% faster than new/delete C++.
what_it_does: A row from benchLANG, a small 19-language benchmark, not a library. The binary-trees workload builds a depth-19 stretch tree, a depth-18 long-lived tree and then 2^(22-d) short-lived trees at each even depth d from 4 to 18 (68,332,206 nodes in all, counted from the loop bounds), sums each with a recursive check and drops it. The OCaml version is a variant type `Node of tree * tree * int` with `Empty` leaves in one bench.ml, compiled ahead of time by ocamlopt into a native executable, plus a 10-line C stub (monotonic.c) because the OCaml stdlib has no monotonic clock. Using the result means writing the allocation-heavy part in OCaml; nothing here links into a C++ program.
how_it_is_fast: Memory management, not code generation; there is no JIT, ocamlopt is an AOT compiler. Likely mechanism (inference, consistent with the README's 'GC runtimes collect when they like'): each Node is a 4-word block (header plus three fields, 32 bytes, the same as glibc's chunk for the C program's 24-byte struct) bumped out of the minor heap, and a minor collection copies only live blocks, so short-lived trees of depth 14 or less (at most 1 MiB, below the default 256k-word or 2 MiB minor heap, Minor_heap_def 262144 in OCaml 5.4.1's runtime/caml/config.h) are never traced or freed one by one. The C and C++ programs call malloc or operator new per node and then walk every tree again (free_tree) to free or delete each node inside the timer. Per node that is about 12.7 ns for OCaml against 14.8 ns for C and 16.8 ns for C++ (derived from page data over 68.3M nodes).
when_to_use: You already write OCaml (compilers, provers, symbolic tools) and wonder whether a pass that builds many short-lived immutable tree nodes should move to C: with default GC settings the native OCaml binary beat naive malloc/free C here.
Workloads that allocate whole trees or ASTs and drop them before the next minor collection, which is the case the generational minor heap makes nearly free.
You want a single native executable (1039 KiB stripped here) with GC-speed allocation and no JIT warm-up or separate VM install, unlike the Java, C# and Bun rows of the same table.
As a data point that per-node malloc/free, not the language, is the bottleneck of a naive C or C++ tree builder.
when_not_to_use: As evidence that OCaml beats tuned C or C++: benchLANG has no arena or pool variant, and a per-tree bump arena or std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource would remove both the per-node frees and the second traversal (inference, not measured here). Benchmarks Game search snippets (pages not opened, different runs and multicore programs, directional only) list gcc #2 with APR pools at 1.56 s against an OCaml 5.2.0~alpha1 program at 3.41 s.

Compute-bound or recursion-heavy code: the same OCaml program loses Fibonacci(45) (4.897 s vs 1.694 s for C), strings (5.000 s vs 2.132 s), primes (3.200 s vs 2.725 s) and Mandelbrot (2.271 s vs 2.201 s), and the suite overall (16.233 s vs 9.762 s, 1.66x slower).
Memory-constrained deployments: whole-process peak RSS was 89.7 MiB for OCaml against 33.3 MiB for C and 35.4 MiB for C++.

Workloads whose trees outlive the minor heap: here the depth-16 and depth-18 short-lived trees (4 and 16 MiB), the stretch tree (32 MiB) and the long-lived tree (16 MiB), about 18.3M of 68.3M nodes (27%), are too big for the default 2 MiB minor heap and must be promoted and later swept by the major GC (derived from the source and runtime defaults); programs with large live data pay more of that cost.
If you just want the biggest allocation-throughput win from a GC runtime: in the same table Java (0.347 s), Nim (0.809 s) and Bun (0.816 s) beat OCaml, and Dart AOT ties it at 0.865 s.

integration.dependencies: OCaml 5.4.1 from nixpkgs-unstable (the plain `ocaml` attribute, i.e. ocamlPackages_5_4, at the flake.lock rev e8be7818) and a C compiler for the monotonic.c clock stub; no opam packages
integration.min_toolchain: OCaml 5.4.1 as measured; bench.ml uses only the Stdlib and one external C stub, so other OCaml releases should compile it, but only 5.4.1 (non-flambda) was measured
integration.platforms: Measured on x86-64 Linux only (flake.nix sets system = x86_64-linux), Ryzen 9 5900X locked at 3.5 GHz
integration.thread_safety: Not applicable: single-threaded workload on one OCaml 5 domain

gotchas: Harness asymmetry behind the margin: C and C++ free every node in a second traversal inside the timer, while OCaml stops its timer with the 16 MiB long-lived tree and all promoted garbage from the depth-16, depth-18 and stretch trees still uncollected in the major heap, and the process exits without a final collection. The README states this design ('native code frees inside the timer'), so the row compares allocation strategies, not code generation.

The documented -O3 does nothing: at the pinned nixpkgs rev (flake.lock e8be7818) pkgs/development/compilers/ocaml/generic.nix defaults flambdaSupport to false and top-level ocamlPackages is ocamlPackages_5_4, and in OCaml 5.4.1's driver/main_args.ml -O3 only sets Flambda simplify rounds and inlining arguments. -inline 200 does still raise the Closure-mode inlining threshold (middle_end/closure/closure.ml), so the OCaml row is a plain closure-mode build with bigger inlining, not an optimised Flambda build.

Small, noisy margin from one run: OCaml's 0.865 s is 14% under C's 1.010 s, while the native malloc-based rows running the identical algorithm already spread from 0.986 s (Fortran) to 1.147 s (C++), 16%. run_benchmarks.sh supports --runs N, but the published table is one run, and the raw benchmark_results_*.txt file (with the CPUx column) is not committed (.gitignore ignores everything not re-included, and .txt is not).

Results depend on default GC parameters (2 MiB minor heap, space_overhead 120 per Percent_free_def in config.h); setting a larger minor heap through OCAMLRUNPARAM would keep the 4 MiB depth-16 trees young and likely help this workload, while a smaller one would promote more (inference, not measured). Binary trees runs last in the process, after four workloads that leave little on the heap. Checksums use OCaml's 63-bit int against C's long long; the analyzer exits with an error on any checksum mismatch, and the values here stay far below 2^62.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Among the catalogued benchLANG binary-trees rows OCaml (0.865 s) sits between Bun (0.816 s) and C# (0.931 s) and well behind Java (0.347 s); pick it when you want an AOT native binary with no JIT or VM and a single-threaded GC, and pick the Java or Bun rows (or LangArena's Java and Bun Binarytrees::Obj entries, which also include stronger C++ baselines) when the size of the margin matters.
verified_claims_summary: benchLANG's 3 September 2026 run on a Ryzen 9 5900X locked at 3.5 GHz (Arch Linux, 48 GB DDR4-3600) timed binary trees at 0.865 s for OCaml 5.4.1 (ocamlopt, non-flambda, default GC) against 1.010 s for C and 1.147 s for C++, both built by GCC 16.2.0 with -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops and allocating each node with malloc/free or new/delete; about 1.17x and 1.33x faster (derived from page data), one run each, with the analyzer checking that every language printed the same checksum.
status_note: Small single-author MIT repo (8 stars, 0 forks, 42 commits, last commit 2026-09-03) with Nix-pinned toolchains and a committed flake.lock, so anyone can rerun it, but this is one run of one micro-workload, not something to adopt as a library.
